Case/data description: Jobat data

Jobat is a Belgian website where you can find a lot of job vacancies: https://www.jobat.be/en

Your job is to scrape the website and explore the vacancies that are currently published.

You can scrape the webpage in Dutch or in English.

library(htmltools)
library(rvest)
library(tidyverse)
library(httr)

1. Webscraping 1.0

  1. Are you allowed to scrape data from the Jobat website? Explain in detail how you have checked this and what is or is not allowed to be scraped from this website.

Answer: In order to check whether we are allowed to scrape data from the Jobat website, we visited https://www.jobat.be/robots.txt to check the pages that are allowed to be scraped. Some pages are disallowed. Those pages include: search pages, API endpoints, login pages, and old job or company listings. But the ICT job listings page ’(en/jobs/ict) is not disallowed thus scraping the page is allowed. Certain bots like DataForSeoBot and PetalBot are blocked, although using an individual or a custom browser-like User-Agent ensures compliance with these rules. Therefore, scraping the ICT job vacancies to conduct research is within the guidelines of the website.

  1. At this point, you only scraped the first 50 job vacancies. Now, loop over the different pages, scraping all ICT related job vacancies posted on the website. Save the results in one dataframe. Build in a crawl delay of 10 seconds.

a) How many job vacancies have you extracted?

The total ICT Job titles extracted were 111. This indicates that the loop and crawl delay worked perfectly and captures all available job related job titles postings from the website.

Answer: 111

Note: In our initial attempt to scrape the ICT job vacancies, the default page URLs ( ?p=) returned 0 results. After reviewing the website structure, we realized that the ICT job vacancies pages are 3 and the page URLs use the ?pagenum= format. We updated the URLs using the pagenum format, and the loop successfully extracted all job titles as required. The following function-based loop successfully scraped all ICT job vacancies across the three pages.

# writing Function to scrape one page
scrape_page <- function(url) {
  
  # Sending request with user-agent
  req <- GET(url,
             user_agent = "paulmariemutamba.mweni@student.kuleuven.be, Moustafa.basiony@student.kuleuven.be, tolulopeolaide.soetan@student.kuleuven.be, evgeniia.shadrina@student.kuleuven.be; Assignment class collecting and analysing big data"
  )
  
  # If request fails, doing a break
  if (status_code(req) != 200) {
    cat("Failed to load:", url, "\n")
    return(character(0))
  }
  
  # Reading the page
  page <- read_html(req)
  
  # Extracting job titles
  titles <- page %>% 
    html_nodes("h2.jobTitle a") %>%
    html_text(trim = TRUE)
  
  # printing the titles back from the function
  return(titles)
}

# creating empty vector to store all job titles
all_titles <- c()

# Total number of pages to scrape (as discovered)
total_pages <- 3

# Looping over pages
for (page_num in 1:total_pages) {
  
  # Building page URL
  if (page_num == 1) {
    url <- "https://www.jobat.be/en/jobs/ict"
  } else {
    url <- paste0("https://www.jobat.be/en/jobs/ict?pagenum=", page_num)
  }
  
  # Displaying which page is being scraped
  cat("Scraping page:", page_num, "\n")
  
  # Scraping job titles
  titles <- scrape_page(url)
  
  # Adding titles to the empty vector created
  all_titles <- c(all_titles, titles)
  
  # Sleep timer
  Sys.sleep(10)
}

b) Preprocess the job titles and make a wordcloud. Explain your preprocessing steps.

Preprocessing Steps:

For preprocessing of the scraped job titles before creating the wordcloud, we performed some standard text-cleaning steps. We converted all text to lowercase, removed punctuation, removed numbers, removed common stopwords such as “the”, “and”, “with”, etc since all these words do not provide any meaningful information. Also, we removed extra whitespaces, tokenized the words, i.e. split them into single words, and calculated the word frequencies to prepare the data for making the wordcloud.

Preprocessing the job titles:

titles <- df2$title

titles_clean <- titles %>%
  str_to_lower() %>%                       # Converting to lowercase
  str_replace_all("[[:punct:]]", " ") %>%  # Removing punctuation
  str_replace_all("[0-9]", " ") %>%        # Removing numbers
  str_squish()                             # Removing extra whitespaces

# Converting to dataframe for tidytext
titles_df <- data.frame(title = titles_clean, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Tokenizing words
tidy_titles <- titles_df %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, title)

# Removing common stopwords
data("stop_words")
tidy_titles <- tidy_titles %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

# Counting word frequencies
word_freq <- tidy_titles %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

Making a Wordcloud for the job titles:

set.seed(123)

wordcloud(words = word_freq$word,
          freq = word_freq$n,
          min.freq = 1,
          max.words = 100,
          random.order = FALSE,
          colors = brewer.pal(8, "Dark2"))

The word cloud depicts the most frequently occurring terms in the ICT job titles. The size of each word corresponds to how often it occurs: larger words, such as engineer, developer, senior, support etc. indicate roles that are widely represented. In contrast, smaller words like web, cybersecurity, freelance etc appear less frequently, suggesting they are less common across the job listing. Overall, the word cloud offers a clear visual summary of the dominant roles and themes within ICT job titles.

c) What are the most common collocations in the jobtitles?

# Creating bigrams (2-word collocations)
bigrams <- titles_df %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, title, token = "ngrams", n = 2)

# Separating the two words
bigrams_separated <- bigrams %>%
  separate(bigram, into = c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ")

# Removing stopwords in either word
bigrams_filtered <- bigrams_separated %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word,
         !word2 %in% stop_words$word)

# Counting bigram frequencies
bigram_counts <- bigrams_filtered %>%
  unite(bigram, word1, word2, sep = " ") %>%
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)

2. Webscraping 2.0

  1. Scrape the jobtitles, location of the position (Antwerp, Brussels…), type of contract (permanent, freelance, fixed-term…), and the salary range for all jobs in ICT. Make one dataframe including all four features (‘jobtitle’, ‘location’, ‘contract’, ‘salary’).

Tip: If you scrape all four features separately and merge afterwards, your merge will be messy. For example: for some jobtitles, the salary range may be missing, but will not be automatically filled with ‘NA’ but with the salary range of the next hit. A solution is to scrape the full job description first and then parse the different elements from that jobdescription. This way, automatic NA will appear where needed.

ictjobtitles <- ict_page %>% html_nodes(".jobTitle a") %>% html_text()
full_job_description <- ict_page %>% html_nodes(".open") %>% html_text()

In this initial exploration, we extract two key pieces of information from the first page of ICT job listings:

Job Titles (ictjobtitles): We use the CSS selector .jobTitle a to target all hyperlinks within elements that have the class “jobTitle”. Full Job Descriptions (full_job_description): We use the .open selector to capture the complete job card information. Each job card contains multiple pieces of information (title, location, contract type, salary)

parse_job_card <- function(raw_text) {
  
  # Split the raw string by new lines and remove whitespace/empty lines
  lines <- raw_text %>%
    str_split("\r\n") %>%
    unlist() %>%
    str_trim() %>%
    discard(~ .x == "") # Remove empty strings
  
  # --- EXTRACTION LOGIC ---
  
  # Title: Typically the first non-empty line
  title <- if(length(lines) >= 1) lines[1] else NA
  
  # Contract: Search for specific keywords
  # We look for the index of the line that contains the contract type
  contract_types <- "(Permanent|Freelance|Fixed-term|Student job|Internship|Starter|Interim|Self)"
  contract_index <- which(str_detect(lines, regex(contract_types, ignore_case = TRUE)))[1]
  
  contract <- if(!is.na(contract_index)) lines[contract_index] else NA
  
  # Location: 
  # Heuristic -> In this HTML structure, Location is usually the line immediately BEFORE Contract
  location <- if(!is.na(contract_index) && contract_index > 1) {
    lines[contract_index - 1]
  } else {
    NA
  }
  
  # Salary: Search for currency symbol
  salary_index <- which(str_detect(lines, "€"))[1]
  salary <- if(!is.na(salary_index)) lines[salary_index] else NA
  
  # Return as a one-row tibble
  tibble(
    Title = title,
    Location = location,
    Contract = contract,
    Salary = salary
  )
}

df_jobs <- map_dfr(full_job_description, parse_job_card)

# 3. View Result

This AI-generated function reliably extracts the four required variables from each job card by using the actual textual structure of the “.open” div.

How the function works:

Text splitting: The raw text is split by line breaks (), trimmed of whitespace, and empty lines are removed. This gives us a clean vector of text lines to work with.

Feature extraction using different strategies:

Title: Assumes the first non-empty line is always the job title

Contract type: Uses pattern matching with regex to search for keywords like “Permanent”, “Freelance”, “Fixed-term”, etc.

Location: Exploits the HTML structure where location consistently appears on the line immediately before the contract type

Salary: Identifies lines containing the euro symbol (€)

Handling missing data:

Each extraction includes conditional logic (if-else statements) to assign NA when information is absent.

dfs=list()
for (i in 1:3){
  url = paste0("https://www.jobat.be/en/jobs/ict?pagenum=", i)
  r = GET(url,
    user_agent="paulmariemutamba.mweni@student.kuleuven.be, Moustafa.basiony@student.kuleuven.be, tolulopeolaide.soetan@student.kuleuven.be, evgeniia.shadrina@student.kuleuven.be; Assignment class collecting and analysing big data")
  page = read_html(r)
  
  full_job_description <- page %>% html_nodes('.open') %>% html_text()
  
  df_jobs <- map_dfr(full_job_description, parse_job_card)
  
  dfs[[i]] <- df_jobs
  
  Sys.sleep(10) 
}

This loop systematically scrapes multiple pages of ICT job listings while following ethical web scraping practices. We iterate through 3 pages to collect all of ICT positions without overburdening the server.

How the loop works:

URL construction: For each iteration, we dynamically build the URL by appending ?p agenum= followed by the page number (1, 2, 3) Polite requests: Each GET request includes our user agent string identifying ourselves and the academic purpose of our scraping

Data extraction: Each page’s dataframe is stored in a list (dfs\[\[i\]]), which we’ll later combine into one dataset. Sys.sleep(10) pauses execution for 10 seconds between requests, respecting the website’s resources and avoiding server overload.

Why we used a for loop instead of a while loop: Known iteration count, we know exactly how many pages we want to scrape (3 pages, which are the entire website at the time of scraping). A for loop is ideal when the number of iterations is predetermined, whereas while loops are better suited for situations where you continue until a condition is met (e.g., “scrape until there are no more pages available”). With a for loop, we have guaranteed termination after exactly 3 iterations, preventing accidental infinite loops that could burden the server. If we are to build a general webscraper that is not affected as time passes and number of postings change, a while loop is more efficient.
